reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: The name captures the triad of hair (tricho-), nose (rhino-), and digit (phalangeal) abnormalities
Characteristic features are sparse, slow-growing scalp hair, a bulbous pear-shaped nose, and a long flat philtrum
The hallmark radiographic finding is cone-shaped epiphyses of the phalanges, leading to shortened fingers and deviation of the digits
Type I is caused by TRPS1 variants; type III is a more severe TRPS1 phenotype with pronounced brachydactyly and short stature
Type II (Langer-Giedion syndrome) results from a contiguous deletion involving TRPS1 and the adjacent EXT1 gene, adding multiple cartilaginous exostoses and intellectual disability
Premature degenerative joint disease of the hands and hips can develop
Hip abnormalities resembling Perthes disease may occur
Diagnosis is clinical and radiographic, confirmed by TRPS1 testing or deletion analysis; management is supportive and orthopaedic
reference.pathophysiology: Trichorhinophalangeal syndrome is caused by loss of function of TRPS1, a zinc-finger transcription factor that regulates chondrocyte and perichondrial development and other aspects of skeletal and ectodermal patterning. Reduced TRPS1 activity disturbs growth-plate function, producing the characteristic cone-shaped epiphyses, brachydactyly, short stature, and hip abnormalities, and also affects hair follicle development, giving the sparse fine hair. Type I arises from intragenic TRPS1 variants, while type III reflects variants with a more severe skeletal effect. Type II (Langer-Giedion syndrome) is a contiguous gene deletion that removes both TRPS1 and the neighbouring EXT1 gene, so the exostoses and cognitive impairment reflect loss of EXT1 in addition to the TRPS1 phenotype.
additionalInvestigations: Hand and skeletal radiographs demonstrating cone-shaped epiphyses
Chromosomal microarray or deletion analysis for suspected Langer-Giedion syndrome
Hip imaging for degenerative or Perthes-like change
Developmental assessment where type II is suspected
redFlags: Nerve or spinal-cord compression from exostoses in Langer-Giedion syndrome
Malignant transformation of an exostosis (rare) with new pain or growth
Progressive disabling hip or hand arthropathy
Significant developmental delay prompting evaluation for type II
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy is normal; morbidity arises from short stature, hand deformity, and early degenerative joint disease, with additional risks from exostoses and cognitive impairment in the Langer-Giedion form.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnostic cone-shaped epiphyses on hand radiographs
Failing to distinguish type II (contiguous deletion with exostoses) from types I and III
Attributing the sparse hair to an isolated ectodermal disorder
Not arranging surveillance of exostoses in Langer-Giedion syndrome
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
management: Recognise there is no disease-specific drug therapy, so care is supportive and directed at the skeletal, ectodermal and, in type II, exostosis manifestations
Manage hip disease and premature degenerative joint disease of the hands and hips with physiotherapy, analgesia and orthopaedic surgery including joint replacement where indicated
Monitor growth and short stature and assess through paediatric endocrinology, with hand therapy for brachydactyly and digital deformity

In Langer-Giedion (type II) disease, monitor and surgically excise symptomatic osteochondromas, remaining alert to malignant change, and provide developmental and educational support for intellectual disability
Offer dermatological and trichological advice for sparse, slow-growing hair, including camouflage or hairpieces
Coordinate care across clinical genetics, orthopaedics, endocrinology and dermatology
Provide genetic counselling and offer family screening with TRPS1 testing, or deletion and microarray analysis where the contiguous-gene form is suspected
